recognized_text: Sir, field report number two on the electricity file. Today, where electricity is made and how it gets home. Last time we learned its charge moving in a wire. Billions of humans each pressing switches whenever they like and someone must supply exactly that at that instant. No more, no less. In 1831, an Englishman named Faraday found something simple. Move a magnet past a wire and its electrons move. Spin the magnet inside a coil of wire and it keeps pushing the electrons back and forth. That's a generator. So naturally it makes AC. A motor is the same machine in reverse. Feed it power, it spins. The fan, the washing machine, the electric car, generators running backwards. Faraday was a blacksmith's son who left school early. A bookbinder's apprentice who read what he bound. Their greatest invention? A guy reading on the job. One question left. Who turns the magnet? They mount it on a giant fan called a turbine. Since Faraday, most of the planet's power is made this same way. All the changes, what turns the turbine. Their favorite way? Boil water. Burn coal or gas under a boiler the size of a building, steam spins the turbine, the turbine spins the generator, out comes electricity. The nuclear plant sir? The most complex thing they ever built. They split the atom itself to boil water. A fingertip of nuclear fuel holds about a ton of coal's energy. Countries with volcanoes take steam straight from underground. Still steam. This planet is addicted to kettles. So, kind one is steam. Coal, gas, nuclear. Kind two is water. A high dam, the water falls onto the turbine. The planet's biggest station, a dam in China. Kind three is wind. Turbines the wind keeps turning. The one exception, the solar panel. Nothing spins at all. Light knocks the electrons and moves them. And it makes direct current. Here's each one's share of the planet's power in 2025. Coal's still first, a third. Then gas, then dams, nuclear, solar, and wind. But that year, for the first time in a century, all renewables together passed coal, by a hair. Solar alone was about 1% 10 years ago. Now, nearly nine. Their fastest growing source is the only one that doesn't spin. Now, let's follow the power. The generator makes it at about 20,000 volts. First stop, a transformer lifts it to hundreds of thousands. The transformer has no moving parts, two coils of wire around iron. More turns on one side, so the pressure comes out higher there. That's it. Then it travels on tall towers, hundreds of kilometers. Near the city, another transformer brings it down. Then smaller ones on the streets until it enters the house at 110 or 240 volts, depends on the country. Both its feet are on the same wire. Current flows when there's a pressure difference between two points. Both feet are at the same pressure. So, no current goes through it. But if it touches another wire or anything grounded at the same moment, it becomes the path. And humans stand on the ground all the time. So, that rule is for birds only. So, what stations make must equal what people draw every second. One number tells them if the balance is right, the frequency. Control orders a station up, the number comes back. All day long, nobody notices. Every grid has a control room, people at screens 24 hours a day. Their whole job, keep that number at 50. The planet's most important workers, and nobody knows their names. The generators help too. Each is hundreds of tons of spinning iron. If something fails, the weight keeps spinning a few seconds, buying the grid time. If a big station drops out and the number falls fast, the grid cuts whole districts by itself. It sacrifices a part, so the whole doesn't fall. Their whole civilization rests on one number. It must stay 50, not 49. It makes for strange moments. In 1990, England played Germany in the World Cup semifinal and went to penalties. The match ended and the whole country got up at once to switch on the kettle. Demand jumped 2,800 MW in minutes, two big power stations, still the record. Their grid engineers have studied the TV schedule ever since. They know when the show ends and have a station ready for that second. England lost the match, the grid won. Grids grew and joined up. Europe, one grid from Portugal to Turkey, over 400 million people. Every generator in it turns together, same speed, same instant. Thousands of machines, like one machine. That makes it stronger. A station fails in one country, the neighbors cover. It also makes the neighbors' problems yours. They trade power every hour. A windy country sells today and buys tomorrow. In 2018, Kosovo and Serbia argued over who should make up missing power. The whole grid slowed a hair. Instead of 50, 49. 996. Oven clocks and alarm clocks, which count time from the grid's pulse, fell 6 minutes behind. In 25 countries, a quarrel between two made a whole continent late for work. Finally, a scientific excuse. Japan is the opposite. In 1895, Tokyo bought German generators turning at 50. The next year, Osaka bought American ones at 60. To this day the country is split in two, joined only by special converter stations. In 2011, after the great earthquake, the east needed power and the west had extra. Only a trickle could cross the link. Tokyo had rolling blackouts. The purchase made over a century ago the changes through the day. The rising in the morning, highest after sunset, when everyone gets home and switches everything on. So some stations run all the time and others sit idle and run just 2 hours a day for the peak. Their power is the most expensive. The year's top peak comes with a heatwave every air conditioner at once or a cold snap. So the grid is built for the worst hour of the year and half of it sits idle the rest of the time. That's why in many countries power prices change by the hour. A washing machine at midnight costs less than one at sunset. Two words from the human dictionary. Hertz, turns per second, the grid's pulse. And megawatt, a million watts, enough for hundreds of homes, or one small data center. Report summary, sir. One, a generator is a spinning magnet, and nearly every station is looking for something to spin it. Two, the voltage goes up, so power can travel, and comes down before the house. Three, what's made must equal what's drawn every second. Same warning, any wire in the street, fallen or hanging, nobody goes near it. Keep away and report it.
